content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors focus on the real-world problem of inapplicable actions, which means that the action cannot be executed in the current state and thus the agents stays in the current state. The authors experimentally verify that the learning process will be faster and more effective if the agent can select the corresponding executable action in different states. The authors also propose to learn the applicability function to distinguish whether an action can be executed or not, and experimentally verify that it can be migrated to different tasks in the same environment.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
* The authors' concern exists in many reinforcement learning implementation scenarios, and the problem has practical value
* The authors' experiments are more adequate and the analysis is clear

Weaknesses.
* The method section is vague and lacks some details. For example, I did not find how to train applicability function in the paper and appendix.
* From what I have learned, the framework proposed by the authors lacks novelty and is more like a summary of existing methods, such as AEN, which is also a common approach when implementing reinforcement learning applications in practice.
* The approach proposed by the authors mainly uses whether the next state is the same as the current state to determine whether it is an action that can be executed. Note that there are factors in some environments that are not controlled by the agent, such as the presence of other entities that may move randomly, which means that it is not possible to use the state to make a judgment about whether the action is feasible. A similar phenomenon is also widespread in multi-agent problems, where multiple agents take actions at the same time.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2447 by Reviewer q3BH

content.title: Answer to Reviewer q3BH's comments
content.comment:
We appreciate the reviewer q3BH's input and comments.
 
The method to train the applicability function is explained in Section 3.2. "The task of learning the applicability function can in fact be reduced to learning a classifier $C_{\phi}$, parameterized by $\phi$, that returns the probability for an action $a$ to be applicable in a given state $s$". We also provide the details of how to train simultaneously the policy and the classifier in Algorithm 1. The architecture of the neural network used can be found in Appendix B.
 
The proposed approach focuses on learning how to identify inapplicable actions in a **task agnostic way with the aim to transfer the knowledge acquired to new tasks** and help speed up the training on these. On the other hand, AEN remains task-focused and aims at identifying sub-optimal actions to solve a specific task. They do not propose any approach to transfer the knowledge acquired to new domains. The closest work to ours on the knowledge transfer approach would be Fernandez et al. (2010), but here as well, the expert policies used are biased towards the task they were trying to achieve.
 
We have generalized the definition of inapplicable action (Definition 3.1) by introducing a distance measure $d(s_{t+1}, s_t)$ allowing more flexibility to identify whether an action had an effect on the environment. We have also explicitly mentioned the limitation associated with our approach in the paragraph after Definition 3.1. Our paper wanted to emphasize more on the ability to transfer the knowledge from one environment to another but the process of learning the inapplicability function could be explored further into more advanced configurations of the environment (i.e non deterministic, partially observable, ...).

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an approach that restricts the action space by learning a mask for "inapplicable" actions, or those actions that, based on the current context, will not contribute toward achieving the desired outcome. The hypothesized contribution of this masking of the action space is that it improve efficiency by eliminating actions from consideration while exploring within the environment. Beyond the training (and use) of this masking function within a single domain, it is demonstrated that the previously learned function can be useful in related domains.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

The proposed "inapplicable action" classifier is an elegant solution to a problem that persists across a large number of complex real-world settings where RL may be used. The simplicity of learning a state-based classifier over whether an action should be considered or not as an auxiliary task is really neat.

While others may clamor for more complex environments, I really appreciate that the authors paid particular focus to simple grid world environments of increasing complexity to test the proposed approach. I think that this belies some of the limitations of the current formulation (more on that below) but it does provide for a much better paper when introducing new ideas to focus on simpler experiments. 

The proposed auxiliary classifier is general in purpose. There's no reason why it shouldn't work in value-based RL although it was only demonstrated with a policy gradient approach. A similar approach, yet focused on risk/safety, using value-based algorithms is: 
```Fatemi, M., Sharma, S., Van Seijen, H., & Kahou, S. E. (2019, May). Dead-ends and secure exploration in reinforcement learning. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 1873-1881). PMLR.```

## Weaknesses

The major weakness of the proposed method is that, as presented, it requires pretty restrictive assumptions about the environments for it to work as intended. As far as I understand, the assumptions are that: 
  1)  Stationary and Deterministic Dynamics
  2) There are no unobserved temporal processes that influence state transitions
  3) Full observability
  4) Discrete action and observation space

While not back-breaking, these are critical assumptions that are not discussed at all in the paper. This severely limits the applicability of the proposed method as it depends strongly on subsequent states being differentiated after an action is taken in order to determine whether or not those actions are applicable. If there is any sort of underlying temporal process that perturbs the state (e.g. wind or drift in navigation envs; physiological factors in health envs) inapplicable actions wouldn't be identified in the current formulation because the state observations are not static event if no action is taken. Similar failure modes exist when considering continuous states or actions. This could be remedied somewhat by defining a minimum $\varepsilon$-ball within which state similarity is determined...

It's unclear how the action samples are rebalanced in Alg 1. There is a reference to line 11 but this doesn't actually give any additional information about why&how this is done.

It's unclear why the exploration term $\epsilon$ is not decayed through time when learning. This isn't a big deal but I wonder if there's not some added efficiency that's been left on the table by maintaining the same frequency of learning/querying the action mask (lines 23-27 in Alg 1) throughout training. Epsilon decay (or at least reduction) is provided when doing transfer between environments, why not when training from scratch too?

It's not clear what the major differences are between Q1 and Q2 in Section 4. More detail or discussion here would better motivate the chosen experiments later in the section. There's a subtle conceptual difference between the 2 questions that should be made more apparent.

At the end of Section 4.1 there is some analysis of the efficiency gains when using privileged information. I was really hoping that similar types of efficiency analyses were done when that type of information was learned from the environment. For instance, 74% of  possible state-action pairs were pruned when the "oracle" provided information. What was the similar kind of efficiency gained when the "inapplicable action mask" was learned?

The "Average Reward" figures (Figs 2, 3a, 5, 6) appear to be normalized by maximum obtained reward. This should be mentioned and made explicitly clear. As should the term "average". Does it mean that multiple episodes are run at each evaluation time?

The terminology "hand-coded" is often used interchangably with the learned action classifier. This introduces some confusion over whether or not the "inapplicable" actions are learned without privileged (or biased) information from humans. This is important to clarify as concerns about whether the human designer needs to specify what's applicable and what's not severely limits the scalability of the algorithm. If this is the intention of the authors, it should be specified. But since there is no real mention or focus on "safety", I have doubts that this is what the authors have considered.

In Section 4.3, it's unclear where the pre-trained classifier for the actions is coming from. It took me several passes through the section and the corresponding figure to fully understand which domain/environment the classifier was trained in.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is well-written and clear for the most part. Areas of concern where things were not clear or were otherwise confusing have been identified in the above section.

In terms of significance (combining notions of "quality" and "novelty") this paper appears to be the first that learns to differentiate between applicable and inapplicable actions without requiring explicit hand-coded associations as such, albeit in limited settings. I wish that more focus was paid to the literature in RL safety but I recognize that the intention of the authors may have been to focus on learning efficiency in more general RL problems. This is an unfortunate consideration as the overall motivation of using an action mask to avoid suboptimal behaviors is a really important thing to consider, see:

```Fatemi, M., Killian, T. W., Subramanian, J., & Ghassemi, M. (2021). Medical Dead-ends and Learning to Identify High-risk States and Treatments. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 34, 4856-4870.```

Thanks to the simplicity of the overall approach, the methods introduced in this paper are easily reproducible. The inclusion of the code used for this paper as well as descriptions in the paper (and appendix) also contribute to this.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a good paper and should be published in my estimation. I am cautious to enthusiastically recommend this without some improvements to the writing and overall discussion in the paper. I've highlighted specific areas in my review where these things could be remedied or at least more transparently discussed (e.g. the assumptions limiting the use of the method). I'm interested to follow the coming discussion with the authors with a refreshed perspective and see if I can increase my rating for this paper.

content.title: Answer to Reviewer HWfy's comments
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer HWfy for the thorough review and good feedback.
 
This approach could indeed work with a value-based RL approach as the concept of masking actions also works with value-based RL algorithm (Even-Dar et al., 2006).
 
We decided to take an approach slightly different than what is traditionally done in the risk/safety literature and avoid reward shaping and attribute a bad reward to inapplicable actions. This lets us limit the amount of domain knowledge required to solve the problem.
 
We have taken onboard the feedback and made the definition of inapplicable actions (Definition 3.1) more general, with the introduction of a distance function to evaluate whether two states should be considered as similar. We have also clarified some of the assumptions of our approach in the paragraph after the definition. The concept of action masking assumes a discrete action space therefore, in this paper we consider an MDP with a discrete action space (section 2). The observation space needs not be discrete, in particular with the generalization of the inapplicable action definition and the introduction of the distance measure. Full observability per se is not a requirement for this approach to work. However the agent must be able to observe the parts of the environment a given action has effect on. For instance, assume an agent is in one room and needs to activate a switch to turn on the light in another room. The agent will only need to see the state of the light as opposed to the entire environment in order to evaluate the applicability of the action. Here we decided to focus on the ability to learn and encapsulate knowledge that could be transferred to other domains but the study of more complicated environments with stochasticity could be the object of future research.
 
The rationale behind the rebalancing of applicable and inapplicable actions samples is explained in the last paragraph of Section 3.2. The idea is that with the policy and the classifier improving, the agent takes less and less inapplicable actions, filling the rollout buffer with a big majority of "applicable actions" samples and thus creating a highly imbalanced dataset to train the classifier. Large imbalance can have detrimental effect on the performance of the classifier (Sun et al., 2009), which is why we apply rebalancing. We use a Weighted Random Sampler approach with the weight inversely proportional to the number of samples for each class. We added this information to the last paragraph of Section 3.2.
 
Algorithm 1 provides the option for the developer to do exactly that (l.15). We decided to orient our focus on the ability to acquire some knowledge that could be transferred to other related domains and chose to leave the hyper-parameter tuning for later, given the already good results we obtained with a fixed $\epsilon$. We added an analysis of the effect of the epsilon parameter in Appendix F.
 
In the experimental section, Q1 tries to evaluate whether introducing human knowledge about inapplicable actions helps reduce the sample complexity of the learning. We wanted to show that if we have knowledge (full or partial) about the environment and the applicability of the actions, we can actually improve the performance of the algorithm. There is thus some ground to try to learn this applicability function, and this is what Q2 tries to answer. We have made it clearer in the paper.
 
For each of the experiments, 5 runs were made with 5 different random seeds (Appendix A). We have added to the paper the explanation about the normalized reward (3rd paragraph of Section 4).
 
The experimental section uses hand-coded applicability functions to answer Q1 and Q3. Q1 (Section 4.1) tries to justify the reason why learning the applicability function can be beneficial to improve the performance of the algorithm. In Q3 (Section 4.2.2), we combine both the hand-coded knowledge provided by humans and the learning method, to complete the knowledge that humans did not have.
 
The environment used to train the classifier was the Maze environment, and the knowledge was transferred to all the other domains. We have made this clearer in the setup section of the experiment. (Results section of Section 4.3)

content.title: Thank you
content.comment:
I wanted to quickly leave a comment expressing my gratitude for the thorough response to the concerns raised in my review.

We are in agreement about the limitation of the great majority of safe RL methods not being appropriate for general use. I would still recommend the dead-ends work cited in my original review as it also eschews the requirement on domain knowledge (beyond being able to define clear negative outcomes and abstracting the tasks to a binary -1/+1 reward structure). 

I'm glad that the paper has been made more clear with precise definitions and the assumptions made more apparent at the outset of the paper. I fear that the omission of these elements when the paper was first submitted left space for the reviewers to dismiss the developments proposed in this work. There are clear limitations of the proposed approach but that doesn't discount its utility. 

Unfortunately, it also seems that the simple elegance of the experiments have also been a stumbling block. There is some validity to the concerns raised by the reviewers but I suppose that it could help to demonstrate how the proposed approach could help in progressively harder Key&Door tasks (multiple keys, multiple doors, etc...). On that note, were the key-door in the same position in every episode? Were the maze domains always static? It would be potentially more powerful if your method could address for more dynamic environment definitions (where walls/barriers were generally known to admit inaccessible actions rather than it being wholly a memorization problem of the agent's state...).

content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the optimal control in reinforcement learning via inapplicable action pruning methods. On the theoretical side, the paper finds that current methods studying action space pruning is ad-hoc and not systematic enough. Therefore, it proposes new criterion on the applicability of the actions, and defines applicability function to measure how much the actions are applicable at each state. The inapplicable actions should be dropped out from the environment. On the empirical side, the paper conducts experiments on four synthetic environments to verify the effect of the applicability functions and action pruning. The results show that the applicability function helps reduce the sample complexity to find the optimal policies, and the knowledge of the inapplicable actions can be transferred across environments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
On the positive side, this paper proposes a criterion on whether the action is meaningful at a particular state. It designs the applicability function, and shows that this function can be trained in a supervised manner. Several experiments on four synthetic environments validate the effectiveness of action pruning, and show that it is possible to transfer the knowledge of inapplicable actions from one domain to another.

On the negative side, the major problems of include the diversity of both methods and experiments, and the limited application of inapplicable actions defined in the paper. The diversity problem has multiple levels. First of all, the four environments are hand-crafted, and not general enough. These environments all belong to some path-finding tasks in a specific maze. However, there are plenty of real world tasks with much more complicated transitions. More experiments on the Atari games or Mujoco environments should be conducted to validate the theory. Second, the studied baseline algorithm contains only PPO. More policy gradient methods are required to investigate as a scientific paper. Third, the comparisons between this paper and previous papers are too limited.

The definition of inapplicability is also confusing. Where does the randomness in the definition of applicability function come from? It seems that it should be a deterministic function. Moreover, the actions that keep the state unchanged seem to be inapplicable in various maze environments (just as the synthetic tasks studied in the paper), but they are meaningful in many other tasks. For example, it is an optimal action to stay in the Pong environment if the ball is hitting just to the pad. On the other hand, there are many inapplicable actions that do change the state but make no sense. For example, the agent may traveling along a ring consisting of a subset of states and obtain no rewards on the ring. The agent's goal is to get rid of that ring. These actions that lead the agent to stay in the ring are all inapplicable, but they change the state. Therefore, I do think the definition of inapplicable actions in this paper well motivated.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is in general well written, but the quality of the paper needs improving. It should be easy to reproduce the experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review: Taking the discussions above into consideration, I recommend to reject the paper. This is a suitable paper for term projects, but not for a scientific conference.

content.title: Answer to Reviewer c5jh's comments
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer c5jh for the valuable comments.

The choice of the environments was made to clearly illustrate the concept of inapplicable actions and focus on the technique to learn and transfer the knowledge about the features of the environment that make an action (in)applicable. As discussed in Section 3.3, the ability to transfer the knowledge from one environment to the other requires the environments to share common features that make some actions inapplicable in certain states.
The environments were designed such that the complexity of the task to solve gradually increases (please see also answer to Reviewer 9CRv). Our method allows us to learn the applicability function in a simpler environment and transfer the knowledge acquired to a more complex one. Section 4.3 shows how the information acquired in the Maze environment helps improve the sample efficiency on the other more complex tasks.
 
The action masking approach is sound for all the algorithms from the family of Policy Gradient algorithms as demonstrated in Huang & Ontanon (2022). Given this fact, we only used PPO as a way to demonstrate how the applicability function could be learnt and transferred across various tasks. Our goal was not to prove that masking actions could help the algorithms learn faster but instead show how we could learn which actions to mask.
 
The process of learning the inapplicability function that we propose is related to the approach of Zahavy et al. (2018), although two different algorithms are used (DQN vs PPO). The code to replicate the results is however only available in Lua and for a single environment (Zork), making the comparison difficult.
For the transfer learning approach, Policy Reuse (Fernandez et al., 2010) appears as the most similar technique to ours, with a certain type of knowledge encapsulated into a model that is queried in a new task. It is why we used this approach as a baseline for the transfer learning comparison.
 
The probabilistic nature of the inapplicability function comes from the fact that the dynamics of the environment are not necessarily well understood. Seeing the inapplicability function as a probability allows the introduction of uncertainty in the prediction. In cases where the applicability function is specified by a human for instance, a user might not be confident enough to say that a given action will *always* be invalid in a certain state. Providing a probability caters for a more nuanced decision rule.
The fact that an action might be applicable in one environment and not in another is dealt with by making sure the algorithm keeps exploring as it is discussed in Section 3.3.
For the game of Pong, despite the racket remaining in the same position, the ball will be moving making the state $s$ (i.e. image of the game received by the agent) and $s'$ different. The action of "staying" will therefore not be considered as inapplicable.
Our definition of inapplicable action makes sure to only look at the action that does not modify the state (or only slightly). There might be other sub-optimal actions that can be learnt but that is outside the scope of this paper. To support our transfer learning approach, it is important to keep the knowledge task agnostic. The goal is really to learn the features of the environment that make an action inapplicable. We are not trying to learn how to identify all types of sub-optimal actions.

The current approach looks at a step by step identification of inapplicable actions. The idea of extending the concept to multiple steps (i.e the ring) is an interesting idea that could be the object of future research.

Quality: 

All experimental tasks appear to be in deterministic environments (I see no statement to the contrary). It would be useful to see experiments in stochastic domains, especially with domains that contain actions that keep the agent in the same state with a high probability (but with probability less than 1). 

The environments and tasks are all similar to each other, and lack complexity. 

The experimental task is not an MDP (unless the number of steps taken in the environment is part of the state definition) because the reward given at task completion depends on the length of the path taken. In all figures, a useful additional baseline would be "full knowledge of the inapplicable actions" (as in Figure 1).

It would be useful to see an analysis of the impact of the exploration parameter epsilon on the results. 
 
The paper does not address how relevant this issue is in general, beyond toy domains and games.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2447 by Reviewer 9CRv

content.title: Answer to Reviewer 9CRv's comments
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback.

First, we want to highlight an important contribution of the paper that was not mentioned by the reviewer. Our approach not only shows how to learn action applicability by experience, but we also demonstrate empirically that the knowledge acquired can be transferred to other domains. The fact that the knowledge acquired relies only on the state and is independent of the reward signal (and therefore the goal), makes the inapplicability function learnt transferrable, providing a better sample complexity when learning a new task (Section 4.3).

We have made the definition of inapplicable action (Definition 3.1) more general with the introduction of a distance measure between two states to deal with the fact that 2 states might not be exactly the same. We have added the assumptions of the approach in the paragraph after Definition 3.1. Then in the experiments (Section 4), we explicitly describe the distance function we used in our evaluation.

We agree with the reviewer that the environments used to present our approach remain relatively simple. We decided to use these environments to easily illustrate the concept of inapplicable actions and focus on the ability to transfer knowledge from one environment to another. While it is obvious for humans that trying to go through a wall is a waste of effort thanks to the knowledge acquired over time, it is something that the learning agent needs to learn from scratch. The use of the gridworld environment helps relate and understand that some actions are not worth exploring, providing a good medium to introduce the advantage of learning inapplicable actions and allowing the transfer of the knowledge acquired.
We introduce a certain level of complexity into the environment by treating the problem as a sparse reward problem, where the agent is rewarded only once it reaches the goal. This makes the problem of finding an optimal policy exponentially more difficult as the action space dimension and the number of steps to the goal increase. The need to prune the search space becomes even more apparent in such cases, and the ability to encapsulate the knowledge about inapplicable actions helps reduce the number of actions to consider.
The environments were chosen with an increasing complexity where the first Maze Environment is quite easy to solve once inapplicable actions are known, while the Key & Door Environment requires the agent to understand that it first needs to grab the key before attempting to open the door.
We justify our decision at the beginning of section 4 (last paragraph).

We added to the "inapplicable actions learning" figures (Fig.3, Fig.8, Fig.9, Fig.10) the full-knowledge baseline. For clarity, we have not added it to the other plots.

We added in Appendix F an analysis of the impact of the exploration parameter $\epsilon$. With a higher $\epsilon$ the agent ignores the classifier more often and therefore spends more time exploring inapplicable action. As the exploration rate decreases the sample complexity of the algorithm improves as it leverages the knowledge acquired by the classifier more and therefore focuses mostly on the exploration of applicable actions. With too little exploration however, the classifier is not able to learn effectively and the high number of actions wrongly classified as inapplicable has a negative impact on the RL algorithm making it diverge.

We use a set of toy examples to illustrate the idea of inapplicable actions. However, this is a general concept common to a variety of real world tasks where RL is used. For example in the financial domain, and more particularly trading, an agent should not sell a stock if it is not present in the portfolio; or in robotics, where inapplicable actions range from hitting a wall when moving, to performing grasping operations when an object is not close by. Moreover, as we discuss in the paper (2nd paragraph of the introduction), previous works have tried to encode inapplicable actions knowledge to achieve better exploration performance. However, as far as we know this is the first work that proposes a systematic way of (1) incorporating this type of knowledge into the RL algorithm; and (2) learning it in cases where it is not available.
